# YOCO-U: Universal YOCO for Efficient Depth Scaling

English · [简体中文](../zh/2604.01220.md) · [Back to the list](../../README.md)

<sub>arXiv 2604.01220 · 2026-04-01 · Microsoft Research, Tsinghua University</sub>

<img src="../../assets/glyphs/2604.01220.svg" alt="[Universal Self-Decoder, SWA-512 (10 layers)] x 3 -&gt; Cross-Decoder, shared global KV (10 layers); injection none; KV single-global">

> Loop only YOCO's self-decoder, whose layers use sliding-window attention, so extra depth costs compute while the cross-decoder's global KV is still computed once.

**Category**: Architecture: where to loop, what to share · **Status**: draft (numbers not yet re-checked) · **Impact**: cites 3 · HF upvotes 18

[paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01220)

## Problem

Looping a standard Transformer re-runs every layer, which regenerates KV caches and repeats global attention, so memory and compute grow with depth.

## Method

- Start from YOCO, where an L/2-layer self-decoder with efficient self-attention (SWA by default) produces one global KV cache that every layer of the L/2-layer cross-decoder reads through cross-attention.
- Replace the self-decoder with a Universal Self-Decoder that applies the same L/2 layers T times in sequence (T=3 by default, 2× the total FLOPs of the non-recursive baseline).
- Project the global KV from the final iteration's output, so its size does not depend on T; only the SWA window caches grow with T.

## Loop layout

| Facet | Value |
|---|---|
| Where the loop sits | KV-producing half (CED encoder / YOCO self-decoder) |
| Weight sharing | fully tied |
| Passes in training | fixed |
| Passes at test time | fixed |
| Input injection | none |
| KV cache | one global KV per token |
| Gradient through passes | n/a |
| Origin | trained from scratch |
| FFN | MoE |
| Attention in the loop | hybrid (full + window / linear) |
| Passes (Universal Self-Decoder, SWA-512) | train 3; test 3 |

Section 4.1 model, a 20-layer YOCO with MoE FFNs (1.3B activated, 10B total). The 10-layer self-decoder uses SWA with window 512 and RoPE and is applied T=3 times with shared weights; its final output is projected once into the global KV that all 10 cross-decoder layers (NoPE) read. Each iteration keeps its own window cache. Figure 6 trains separate 1.3B models with 1, 2, 3 and 5 loops.

Section 4.5 states that YOCO-U gives up 5% of YOCO's decoding throughput, decodes 2.21× faster than the Transformer at 256K, and that RINS needs 38× the KV memory of YOCO-U.

## Other findings

- Looping the cross-decoder instead of the self-decoder averages 47.34 (46.41 without the shared KV), against 48.25 for YOCO-U and 46.95 for non-recursive YOCO; the authors conclude that recursion on deeper layers gives diminishing improvement regardless of the KV cache strategy. (Table 5; Section 4.3)
- At about 2× FLOPs, looping the whole 20-layer Transformer twice averages 47.8, while RINS and YOCO-U both reach 48.3; the authors read this as scaling FLOPs on bottom blocks being more effective than on all blocks. (Table 3; Section 4.2; Appendix E)
- Separately trained 1.3B models with 1, 2, 3 and 5 loops show consistent improvements in validation loss as the loop count grows; Loop=5 uses 3 times the FLOPs of the non-recursive model. The figure prints no per-loop values. (Figure 6; Section 4.4)
- YOCO-U trained on 80B tokens is comparable with non-recursive YOCO trained on 210B tokens (approximately 62% fewer tokens). (Figure 2; Section 4.1)
- With training steps fixed, YOCO-U matches YOCO with 50% fewer parameters; when activated parameters are aligned, the authors say YOCO-U narrows the gap to non-recursive models and is near-comparable above 10B. (Figure 5; Section 4.4)
- On Needle-in-a-Haystack, YOCO-U scores 1.00 (S-NIAH-1) and 0.95 (S-NIAH-2), against 0.87 and 0.82 for the Transformer and 0.99 and 0.91 for RINS. (Table 4)

## Comparison

- **Baseline**: Non-recursive YOCO with the same configuration and hyperparameters (Loop=1); Section 4.2 adds a Transformer, a Universal Transformer looped twice, RINS and ParScale at 1.3B dense.
- **Held fixed**: N (unique parameters), A (active parameters), F (training FLOPs)
- **Differs**: D (training tokens), L (executed layers per token), KV (KV cache per token)
- **Baseline hyperparameters**: shared with the looped model
- **Headline claim**: With the same 1.3B-activated / 10B-total MoE, YOCO-U at equal training FLOPs averages 46.23 on the Table 2 tasks against 41.78 for non-recursive YOCO (+4.45), and 47.08 at equal steps; at equal FLOPs its loss is lower by 0.033. (Section 4.1; Table 2; Figure 2)

## Caveats

- The headline runs are a 1.3B-activated / 10B-total MoE trained on up to 300B tokens; the architecture comparison, ablations and loop scaling use 1.3B dense models trained on 20B tokens, and the efficiency tests use the same 1.3B configuration. Training length is 8192 in Sections 4.1 and 4.4.
- Each model is trained and tested with one fixed loop count (3 by default; 1, 2, 3 and 5 in Figure 6); the paper does not report changing the loop count at inference.
- Training FLOPs are computed as tokens × layers (Section 4.1), and the Equal FLOPS row of Table 2 does not state its token count.
- The KV cache is not identical to YOCO's because each self-decoder iteration keeps its own window cache (Table 10, 46 MB vs 26 MB at 8K and 542 vs 522 MB at 256K).
- Prefill throughput is below non-recursive YOCO's, 76301 vs 220407 tokens/s at 256K (Table 8).
- Table 5 does not state the loop count or FLOPs of the Upper Loop variants.
